Good Day Ladies and Gentlemen of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee.
My name is Amy McFarland. I run Independence Farm, a medical cannabis farm with my husband.
Today I am testifying in favor of LD# 1038. (An Act to Increase the Maximum Term of a Medical Cannabis Certification to 2 Years)
By extending the certification term from 1 year to 2 years, patients like myself can save on renewal fees, gas and time. With a terrible economy like ours, every penny counts.
Doctors' offices and hospitals throughout Maine are short staffed and over burdened. If we were to extend the certificates to 2 years, this would help lighten the load on our medical system.
With that said, I ask you all to vote "Yes" on LD# 1038.

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and esteemed colleagues of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee, my name is David Boyer, and I am proud to present L.D. 1038, An Act to Increase the Maximum Term of a Medical Cannabis Written Certification to 2
Years.
For many patients, medical cannabis is a vital tool for managing conditions such as chronic pain, epilepsy, cancer-related symptoms, and PTSD. The current requirement to renew registration annually creates an undue hardship, both financially and logistically.
Patients must schedule appointments with healthcare providers, pay associated fees, and navigate the renewal process every year--tasks that can be especially challenging for those with limited mobility, financial resources, or access to transportation. Extending the registration period to two years would ease these burdens, allowing patients to focus on their health rather than paperwork.
Medical cannabis remains excluded from insurance coverage, leaving patients to bear the full cost, compounded by a 5.5% sales tax--or 8% for edibles--on every purchase. This financial burden adds an extra layer of strain for those already managing chronic conditions. A two-year cycle respects the chronic nature of these conditions while maintaining accountability within the program. Patients deserve a system that works for them, not one that imposes unnecessary obstacles to their care.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.

March 24, 2025
Senator Hickman, Chair Representative Supica, Chair Members, Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs 100 State House Station Augusta, ME 04333-0100
Re: LD 1038 - An Act to Increase the Maximum Term of a Medical Cannabis Written Certification to 2 Years
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs, thank you for the opportunity to provide information in opposition to LD 1038, An Act to Increase the Maximum Term of a Medical Cannabis Written Certification to 2 Years.
LD 1038 seeks to increase the maximum term for a medical cannabis written certification from one year to two years, diminishing the bona fide medical provider:patient relationship on which the written certification is based.
Currently, a written certification for medical cannabis issued by an authorized medical provider under 22 MRS Chapter 558-C is valid for a term of up to one year, as determined by a patient's certifying medical provider. This term ensures regular contact between licensed healthcare providers and qualifying patients. More frequent consultation between a patient and medical provider is important for monitoring a patient's health status. A move to a set two-year term shifts Maine's Medical Use of Cannabis Program (MMCP) further away from having parity with standards of care that exist for prescribed medication, including controlled substances.
Prescribing regulations serve to protect the health and safety of patients and, for MMCP, these safeguards exist through the bona fide relationship1 between healthcare provider and the qualifying patient. The one-year term ensures that, prior to receiving a written certification, the qualifying patient has the opportunity to review with a healthcare professional the person's medical history and current health status and whether cannabis may continue to benefit the person by way of alleviating symptoms, and to be educated on potential health risks of using cannabis, including contraindications.
1 22 MRS �2423-B requires a bona fide provider-patient relationship, that a written certification may be made only in the course of a bona fide medical provider-patient relationship after the medical provider has completed a full assessment of the patient's medical history. If a patient has not provided a medical provider who is not the patient's primary care provider with the name and contact information of the patient's primary care provider, a medical provider shall conduct an in-person consultation with the patient prior to providing a written certification.

According to Maine's Department of Professional and Financial Regulation, Chapter 21: Use of Controlled Substances for Treatment of Pain, which is a joint rule of the Board of Licensure in Medicine, the State Board of Nursing, and the Board of Osteopathic Licensure, a risk assessment of a patient must be performed prior to prescribing or increasing the dosage of any controlled substances for acute or chronic pain. For chronic pain, this risk assessment is to include factors such as personal or family history of substance use disorders, current use of substances, mental health conditions, comorbidities, possible pregnancy, and other conditions. Additionally, periodic reviews of the patient's health and impact of the prescription must be conducted, with the maximum recommended period between reviews to be 12 months for low-risk patients, and more frequently for higher-risk patients.
In conclusion, Maine CDC opposes LD 1038. The annual encounter with a medical provider is valuable to the qualifying patient using cannabis either as an alternative to prescription medication or adjunct treatment. Maine CDC recommends maintaining the current maximum one-year term for written medical cannabis certifications in the interest of patient health and safety, to ensure that the medical provider:patient relationship remains as a safeguard and to better reflect, as a medical program, the standards of care that are in place for prescribed medications.
Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions during your deliberation of this bill.
Sincerely,
Puthiery Va, DO Director Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention Maine Department of Health and Human Services

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs:
The Office of Cannabis Policy (OCP) respectfully submits the following comments neither for nor against LD 1038 to inform this committee's consideration of what it means for Maine to have a medical cannabis program.
At its core, this bill is about whether there is a place for a bona fide relationship between qualifying patients and their certifying medical providers in the Maine Medical Use of Cannabis Program. This question is amplified by the consideration of LD 929, a bill that would permit seniors and veterans to bypass the patient certification process altogether by permitting those individuals to use their photo or veterans ID to obtain medical cannabis.
Nationwide, there are a variety of approaches to ensuring patient access to cannabis for medical use that could inform the committee's work on this issue. Some states, like Oregon, permit qualifying patients to obtain cannabis for medical use from either an adult use or medical use retailer. States like Washington and Vermont permit adult use retailers to obtain a "medical endorsement" to sell medical cannabis to patients out of their adult use location.1 Despite these different approaches and as noted in our testimony regarding LD 929, nearly every medical cannabis program in the country requires a medical provider to certify, at least annually if not more frequently, that a patient has a qualifying condition or would otherwise benefit from the medical use of cannabis. This practice mirrors general prescribing requirements for noncontrolled substances and is much less stringent than the prescription requirements for controlled substances.2 Does this committee believe that medical cannabis requires less oversight than

prescription medications for high blood pressure, ADHD, Type 1 diabetes, or depression? (All of which, coincidentally, can be affected pharmacologically by cannabis use.3)
Taken together, the absence of qualifying conditions, regular assessment and review by a qualified medical provider, mandatory testing for contaminants, and the use of an inventory tracking system in Maine's medical cannabis program present this committee with a fundamental question: What is the purpose and role of the Maine Medical Use of Cannabis Program? Is it the Legislature's intent that the medical cannabis program serves as a sort of cannabis wholesale club (like Costco, Sam's Club, or BJ's) where a patient certification serves as a sort of "membership card" that grants patients access to tax-free cannabis subject to substantially less regulation than cannabis available in the adult use program? If that is the Legislature's intent, does such a system require the maintenance of the kind of robust, distinct, and State-regulated medical cannabis program that OCP has advocated for, and continues to advocate for, before this committee every year?
Finally, there are two issues regarding the certification of qualifying patients that are necessary to understand for the purposes of this discussion. First, the statute requires that certifying providers issue a written certification "only in the course of a bona fide medical provider-patient relationship after the medical provider has completed a full assessment of the patient's medical history..." and further requires in some circumstance that the certifying provider "...conduct an in-person consultation with the patient prior to providing a written certification." 22 MRS � 2423-B(2-C). Second, in accordance with 22 MRS � 2423-B(4), the Office of Cannabis Policy provides, at no charge to certifying providers, the tamper-resistant certification paper that the provider uses for each patient certification (commonly referred to as a "patient card"). The Maine Medical Use of Cannabis Act does not specify or otherwise limit the fees that a certifying provider can charge a patient seeking certification. In the interest of addressing the policy aims of this bill, it may be advisable to review these subsections of � 2423-B to ensure these provisions are in alignment with any changes made to sub-� 3.
In closing, we want to reiterate the Office's strong support for a medical cannabis program that is robust and distinct from the state's Adult Use Cannabis Program; but that program must be wellregulated with the mandatory testing and tracking guardrails necessary to ensure the integrity of Maine's longstanding, and constantly evolving, medical cannabis program. OCP and this committee are regularly asked to treat cannabis businesses the same way we would treat any other business. In this case, then, it is critical that this committee consider the necessary public health and public safety ramifications of changes to the patient certification requirements. We thank the committee for its consideration of our comments and concerns and we would be happy to answer any questions you have at the work session.

I am writing to express my strong support for LD 1038, which proposes extending the maximum term of medical cannabis written certifications from one to two years.
This extension would significantly reduce the administrative burden on both patients and the Office of Cannabis Policy (OCP). Patients would benefit from fewer certification appointments, resulting in reduced costs and increased continuity of care. Simultaneously, the OCP could allocate resources more efficiently, enhancing overall productivity.
Aligning the certification term with the existing two-year renewal period for registry identification cards also promotes consistency within the medical cannabis program, simplifying processes for all stakeholders.

I respectfully urge you to vote Yes on LD 1038 to support these necessary improvements to Maine's medical cannabis program.
186531:
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and the members of the veterans and legal affairs committee. My name is Lizzy Hayes, I am a medical cannabis caregiver and a medical cannabis patient and I am speaking today in support of LD1038 which would extend the term of patient written certifications to 2 years.
Many patients use cannabis to treat chronic and lifelong conditions, and recertification is a step we must take each year to continue to have the right to access, grow and to possess our medicine. Many patients, like myself, grow their own plants, process their own medicine and manage their own care through years of experimenting with various dosages and different strains to get the personalized medicine that best treats their symptoms. Most physicians have no formal training on the use of cannabis as medicine and patients will often get more in-depth recommendations and information from caregivers who are experienced in using cannabis and can advise on ways to consume it carefully or direct them to specific cultivars, and share experiences of other patients dealing with similar symptoms. I see many sincere and knowledgeable caregivers filling a role as community herbalists, and apothecaries where they can supply and advise on the use of this very medicinal plant.
There are other states which allow for longer periods of medical certifications such as Illinois, and Oklahoma which is a 2 year period, or Maryland which allows up to 3 years. And some states have language that allows for a longer period if specified or designated by the physician. This seems especially appropriate in the cases of lifelong incurable conditions such as seizure disorders, pain from permanent physical injury, autism spectrum disorder or other conditions that would require long term ongoing treatment. I ask that this committee please vote ought to pass on a bill that is a very small step to reduce the number of times that a patient must renew their card, and I would ask that you engage in discussions about the appropriateness of extending beyond two years for veterans, seniors or patients with lifelong conditions. Thank you.
And I wanted to address a question asked by Senator Timberlake to Representative Boyer regarding the potency of medical cannabis vs that of adult use and the need for a medical review by a doctor due to the increased potency. Home growers in adult use can make products that are just as potent as the products available on the medical cannabis market.
